newsitem.title: USA: Clinton unveils controversial new clean air rules.
newsitem.headline: Clinton unveils controversial new clean air rules.

text.p: President Bill Clinton announced tough new U.S. air pollution controls on Wednesday, just one day before he goes to a world environmental summit where American policies have been severely criticised.

Speaking in Nashville, Tennessee, Clinton said he had decided to proceed with proposed new controls on soot and smog that have been hailed by U.S. environmental and health groups but blasted by industry and local government.
"I approved some very strong new regulations today that will be somewhat controversial. But I think kids ought to be healthy," Clinton told a family values conference.
"We think if we have high standards for protecting the environment, but we're flexible in how those standards are implemented...that we can protect the environment and grow the economy," he said.

The key architect of the plan, Environmental Protection Agency administrator Carol Browner, said at the White House that the new rules amounted to "a major step forward for protecting the public health of the people of this country."
The White House said the new standards would prevent about 15,000 premature deaths each year from air pollution.
Congress will have 60 days to review the standards, which would be implemented for smog beginning in 2004 and for soot probably at some later date, and may attempt to overturn them.
Under the plan, major producers of smog and soot such as big power plants would be required to meet new lower standards and violators could be severely punished.
A leading U.S. environmental group, The Sierra Club, immediately praised the decision, saying it would lead to cleaner air and improved health.

"Bill Clinton and (Vice President) Al Gore have obviously made the decision to protect the five million American children who suffer from asthma from pollution in our air," said Kathryn Hohmann, a Sierra Club official.
But the plan faces fierce opposition from powerful business and local government groups, including many politicians from Clinton's own Democratic party.
The U.S. Conference of Mayors voted in San Francisco on Tuesday to oppose it, saying the proposed standards would be so costly they could jeopardise local economies.
In a bid to mollify such critics, the White House said the plan would allow polluters several years to comply.

"Those that have opposed the higher standards, I want to just tell you -- read the implementation schedule, work with us. We will find a way to do this ... that grows the American economy," Clinton said.

The announcement came just one day before Clinton addresses a U.N. environmental summit in New York. The United States is being pilloried at the summit as the largest polluter on the planet and for reducing funding for international environmental projects.
